name: Adam Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Adam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'll admit I nearly cancelled, because it's the middle of busy season. But my partner Lena said I complain about this stuff at dinner anyway, so I might as well complain to someone who writes it down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Fair enough. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a senior at Halden & Pike, about forty people, and I run a little team of three doing year-end accounts and tax returns for small businesses. Cafés, a dental practice, two plumbers, a lot of landlords. I'm in by half eight, I review whatever the juniors prepared, and I still tick the working papers in pencil before I sign them off, which everyone teases me about. The best part is the phone call where a client finally understands their own numbers. The worst part is January, when I don't see daylight.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Chasing clients for receipts, honestly. Half my job is getting a man who runs a café to find a shoebox. The other thing is the firm keeps buying new software and expecting us to learn it over a weekend, and I just don't want to. I know how to do this properly already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like the most likely one to me. Every year someone tells us the robots are coming for accountants and every year I'm still finding the café owner's missing VAT receipts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit smugly. At work I'd point out that the partners spent a fortune on the new reconciliation tool and we still do half of it by hand. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something about how the hype was mostly about selling software subscriptions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. I'm good at this job the way it is, and I'd keep being good at it. The only thing that touches me is the routine stuff, the bank matching and the data entry, and that's the juniors' work more than mine. My worry would be them, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly I'd keep going. I'd keep reviewing files the way I do now and keep pushing the partners for the pay rise they half promised me after I qualified. Lena and I want to stop renting in a few years, so I'd keep putting about three hundred a month into the deposit account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit tired, because a world where nothing changes is still a world where January is horrible. But my job is safe and my money's fine, so I can't pretend to be worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd worry about the juniors. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya, who joined in September. She spends most of her week matching bank lines and coding invoices, and that's exactly the bit software is getting decent at. If the firm decides it needs two juniors instead of three, Priya (the newest junior) would go first, and that's not fair because she's sharp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the partners if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight that cutting the junior who's still learning is how you end up with no seniors in five years. Nobody becomes me without spending two years ticking bank statements. I'd say it in the partners' meeting, even if it costs me a bit of goodwill.

say: I'd say the AI hype was mostly about **selling software subscriptions**.
I'd remind the partners the new **reconciliation tool** still leaves half the work to us.
think: My own job is **safe**, because I'm good at it the way it is.
The routine **bank matching** that AI takes is the juniors' work, so my worry is for them.
do: Keep reviewing files by hand and **ticking working papers** in pencil.
Push the partners for the **pay rise** promised after qualifying.
Keep saving about **£300 a month** towards a house deposit with Lena.
feel: **Calm**, because his job and money feel secure.
Still **tired**, since January stays brutal whatever AI does.
S0.quote: Nobody becomes me without spending two years ticking bank statements.
fieldNote: Speaks about his skills with quiet **pride** and a little smugness about the hype fading.
His real concern is **Priya**, the newest junior, not himself.
Already resists the firm's **software purchases** even when they barely work.
Ready to spend **goodwill** with the partners to protect trainees.

steps.text: Keep reviewing his team's year-end files and signing them off by hand
Put about £300 a month into the house deposit account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one is uncomfortable, because 'checking' is on that list and checking is basically what I do all day. Writing the notes to the accounts too. That's not the juniors' work, that's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need rules on this before the partners rush in. I'd push for a proper staff consultation, maybe join the professional body's working group if they have one. With friends I'd say the firms will use it as an excuse to squeeze people and keep the savings for the partners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it means my team shrinks from three to one and I end up reviewing what a machine prepared. Maybe they keep me because I'm good, but they might decide one senior can cover two teams. I don't use any of these tools, so I'd be starting behind people who already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder straight away, probably move the deposit savings up to five hundred a month and cut the takeaways and the weekend trips. I'd join the staff forum and push for a written promise on redundancies. I'd probably wait a while before learning the tools, which I know isn't clever, but I'd want to see what the firm actually buys first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, I've got about four months saved and Lena's job is solid. But I can picture the meeting where they tell me my team is being 'restructured', and I don't like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said learning the tools late isn't clever. Why hold off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly stubbornness, I'll admit it. Partly because every tool they've bought so far has been abandoned within a year, so I don't trust it. And partly because if I'm the one who gets good at the software, I'm the one who helps them cut my own team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena about it that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we can't buy the flat on Mill Road this year. She'd say that nurses have been told their jobs were changing for twenty years and they're still short-staffed. Lena (his partner) would be right, but nurses can't be replaced by a spreadsheet that writes itself.

say: I'd demand a **staff consultation** before the partners rush in.
I'd say firms will use AI to **squeeze staff** and keep savings for partners.
think: My team could shrink **from three to one**, with me checking machine work.
I never use these tools, so I'd start **behind** colleagues who do.
do: Raise deposit savings to **£500 a month** and cut takeaways and trips.
Join the **staff forum** and push for a written redundancy promise.
Hold off learning the tools until the firm picks one.
feel: **Anxious**, picturing the meeting where his team is restructured.
Steadied a little by **four months** saved and Lena's secure job.
S1.quote: If I'm the one who gets good at the software, I'm the one who helps them cut my own team.
fieldNote: Sees that **checking** and writing notes, his core work, are on the card.
Resistance is partly principle: learning tools feels like **helping cut** his own team.
Turns quickly to **collective** protection rather than personal retraining.
Admits his delay is **stubbornness**, which he names himself.

steps.text: Raise the house deposit savings from £300 to £500 a month
Drop the weekly takeaways and weekend trips away
Join the staff forum and ask for a written redundancy promise
Wait to learn the AI tools until the firm commits to one

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two busy seasons. If it can do any thinking work, then preparing a tax return is a joke for it. And the robots coming three years later don't matter to me at all, my job has nothing hands-on in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we needed regulation ten years ago. I'd be loud online for the first time in my life, sharing petitions for a jobs guarantee or some kind of income support. At work I'd say the partners owe the staff a plan, not just a press release.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished as an accountant by 2028 or soon after. Clients will file their own returns through some app that's better than me. Maybe a few people survive signing things off for the tax office, but that's partners, not a 27-year-old senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the flat plan and keep the deposit as an emergency fund, which would turn four months of savings into more like ten. I'd join whatever union or group forms for professional staff and go to the meetings. And I'd look hard at work that needs hands, because those three years before robots are the only gap I can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. Everything I trained for, the master's, the exams, it would all have been for about five years of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of hands-on work did you have in mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something like Lena's world, maybe. My cousin Dev retrained as an electrician at thirty and he's busy all the time. But that's a three or four year apprenticeship, so I'd finish it right as the robots arrive in 2031. I can't see a clean way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go loud online for the first time. What would you actually post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd share the numbers: how many accountants there are, how fast they'd be cut, and who keeps the money. I'd say that if a few software firms get the savings from millions of lost jobs, they should pay for the people left behind. That's the only answer I believe in.

say: I'd say we needed **regulation** of AI ten years ago.
I'd share petitions for a **jobs guarantee** or income support online.
think: I expect to be **finished** as an accountant by 2028 or soon after.
Only **partners** signing for the tax office might survive, not a young senior.
do: Cancel the flat plan and turn the deposit into a **ten-month** emergency fund.
Join a **union** or staff group for professionals and attend meetings.
Look at **hands-on** trades for the three-year gap before robots.
feel: **Alarmed** and losing sleep over losing his career.
**Bitter** that years of exams bought only about five years of work.
S2.quote: Everything I trained for, the master's, the exams, it would all have been for about five years of work.
fieldNote: Fully **desk-based** work means the 2028 date hits him with no robot delay.
Sees the three-year **robot gap** as an escape, then doubts it.
His outlook shows in **who pays**: software firms should fund the people left behind.
First time he'd go **public** online, a big step for him.

steps.text: Turn the house deposit into a ten-month emergency fund
Shelve buying the flat on Mill Road with Lena
Join a staff union for professional workers and attend meetings
Post the job-loss numbers and push for a tax on AI firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better, but only a bit. It's 2031 and I'm 32. It's still the whole thinking side of my job in one go, and there's nothing else to my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still time to do this fairly, if governments move now. At work I'd push for the firm to commit to retraining staff instead of just cutting them. I'd probably say it in the staff forum at every meeting until they got sick of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me time to get out before the door shuts. But it means doing something I really don't want to do, which is change. I'd rather stay put and be good at my job, and I know that's not going to be an option.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep working but save hard, maybe five or six hundred a month, so I've got a year of money by 2029. I'd look into an evening course, maybe teaching, because classrooms still need a person even if AI does the marking. I'd also keep going to every staff meeting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but less trapped than with two years. Five years is enough time to pick something. It's not enough time to pretend it isn't happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum was a maths teacher, and I already spend half my day explaining things to juniors and to clients who hate numbers. It feels like the human bit of my job, not the bit a machine does. The pay is worse, but Lena and I could live on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd rather stay put. What would make you actually start the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing the firm stop hiring juniors. The moment there's no new intake in September, I'd know they've decided. The empty desk where Priya used to sit would be the sign, and I'd sign up that week.

say: I'd say there's still **time to do this fairly** if governments act now.
I'd push the firm to **retrain staff** instead of simply cutting them.
think: Five years gives me time to **get out** before the door shuts.
Leaving means **change**, which I really don't want but can't avoid.
do: Save **£500 to £600** a month to reach a year of money by 2029.
Look into an evening course in **teaching** maths.
Keep raising **retraining** at every staff forum meeting.
feel: **Anxious** but less trapped than with two years.
Clear that five years is enough to **pick something**, not to ignore it.
S3.quote: An empty desk where the junior used to sit would be my sign to sign up for teacher training that week.
fieldNote: The extra time turns **panic into a plan**, but a reluctant one.
Teaching appeals as the **human part** of what he already does.
Needs a hard **trigger**, an empty junior desk, before he'll move.
Still pairs personal steps with **collective** pressure on the firm.

steps.text: Save £500 to £600 a month to hold a year of costs
Research evening teacher training courses in maths
Raise retraining for staff at every staff forum meeting
Start teacher training only once the firm stops hiring juniors

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. That actually changes things, because ten years is a whole career stage. I could still be an accountant for a good while and then move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for governments or firms not to plan. I'd say the professional body should be negotiating now about what happens to people like me. I'd probably be less loud than with two years, because it wouldn't feel like an emergency yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think I can probably do my job for another five or six years and get a lot of experience out of it. Then I'd have to switch. It still means I'll never be a partner, which was the plan, and that stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, honestly, not much. I'd keep working, keep saving three or four hundred a month, and maybe buy the flat with Lena after all, because we'd have time to pay some of it off. I'd keep an eye on it and start a teaching qualification in a few years, not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious in a slower way. It's like knowing your rent will double in ten years. You can plan for it, but it sits there in the back of your head every time you open a tax file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy the flat even knowing your job ends around 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. Lena's nursing job is hands-on and the robots come later still, so her pay probably lasts longer than mine. We'd take a smaller mortgage than we planned, on her salary rather than mine. If I have to retrain at 33, I'd rather do it from a home we own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the partnership plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gone. You don't buy into a partnership that has ten years left. That was the ladder I was climbing since uni, and in this picture the ladder just stops halfway. I'd have to find a new ladder at 33, and I'm not good at that.

say: I'd say a **decade** leaves no excuse for firms or governments not to plan.
I'd want the **professional body** negotiating now for people like me.
think: I can likely keep my job for **five or six years** before switching.
The plan to become a **partner** is gone, and that stings.
do: Keep working and saving **£300 to £400** a month.
Buy the flat with Lena on a **smaller mortgage** sized to her salary.
Plan a **teaching qualification** in a few years, not now.
feel: **Anxious** in a slow, background way, like a rent rise he can see coming.
Unsettled that his **career ladder** stops halfway.
S4.quote: Knowing your job ends in ten years is like knowing your rent will double in ten years. You can plan for it, but it sits there.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **defer** change, which suits his resistant streak.
Leans on Lena's **hands-on** nursing job lasting longer than his.
Loss of the **partnership** dream hurts more than the money.
Admits he's **not good** at finding a new path.

steps.text: Keep preparing and reviewing small business accounts at Halden & Pike
Save £300 to £400 a month alongside the mortgage
Buy the flat with Lena on a mortgage sized to her salary
Put off a teaching qualification for a few more years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't enough to retrain for anything, and I'd be finishing an apprenticeship just as the robots arrived. What would help is money while I retrain, paid by the companies making the savings, and a firm that keeps juniors on so there's still a path in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the juniors much, and I think they're the real story. I'm 27 and senior, so I've got options. The people starting now might never get the training that made me any good. Knowing the work by hand is what lets you spot the mistake a machine misses, and nobody will learn that if the first rung is gone.

headlineQuote: Knowing the work by hand is what lets you spot the mistake a machine misses, and nobody will learn that if the first rung is gone.
portrait: A **27-year-old senior** at a forty-person firm, leading three people on small business accounts and tax.
Proud of doing things **by hand** and refuses to use AI tools, partly from principle.
Calm if AI stalls, **anxious** under slow change, and alarmed by a two-year AGI.
Blames **firms and software makers** and turns to staff groups and politics for answers.
His real fear is the **first rung** of training vanishing for juniors like Priya.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain for anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** funded by the companies making the savings.
Firms that keep hiring **juniors** so there's still a way into the work.
